The difference between bail in bailable and non-bailable offences lies in the legal framework governing their availability and conditions for release.

A "bailable offence" is defined as an offence that is shown as bailable in the First Schedule or made bailable by any other law in force [4(c)]. In such cases, a person accused of the offence may be released on bail without conditions, or with a bond, and the process is generally more accessible. For example, under Section 2(1)(c) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, bailable offences are those listed in the First Schedule or made bailable by other laws [4].

In contrast, a "non-bailable offence" is any offence not falling under the category of bailable offences [4(c)]. For non-bailable offences, bail is not automatically granted and is subject to strict conditions and judicial discretion. According to Section 480(1)(i) and (ii), a person accused of a non-bailable offence may not be released on bail if there are reasonable grounds to believe they committed an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment, or if they have a prior conviction for an offence punishable with imprisonment for seven years or more, or for two or more cognizable offences punishable with imprisonment for three years or more but less than seven years [1].

Additionally, Section 480(3) mandates that when bail is granted for a non-bailable offence, the Court must impose specific conditions, such as attendance as per bond conditions, refraining from committing similar offences, and not tampering with evidence [1].

Moreover, Section 478(1) applies only to persons not accused of a non-bailable offence, indicating that bail for such persons is not governed by the same rules as for those accused of non-bailable offences [6].

Thus, the key difference is that bailable offences allow for release on bail without stringent conditions, while non-bailable offences require judicial discretion, and if bail is granted, it comes with strict conditions and is only permitted under specific circumstances [1][4].

Note: The Information Technology Act, 2000, Section 77B, states that offences punishable with imprisonment of three years or above are cognizable and that the offence punishable with three years’ imprisonment is bailable [5]. However, this does not override the classification under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, which defines bailable and non-bailable offences in Section 2(1)(c) and applies the distinction in the context of bail eligibility and conditions [4].

The difference between bail in bailable and non-bailable offences lies in the availability and conditions of bail, as defined in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

A "bailable offence" is one that is shown as bailable in the First Schedule or made bailable by any other law in force. A "non-bailable offence" means any other offence not specified as bailable [4(c)]. 

In bailable offences, a person accused of the offence may be released on bail without conditions, or with a bond, and such release is generally available at the discretion of the court or officer, especially when the accused is not suspected of a serious offence [478(1)]. 

In non-bailable offences, bail is not automatically granted and is subject to strict conditions. A person accused of a non-bailable offence may only be released on bail if there are no reasonable grounds to believe that the person committed an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment or imprisonment for seven years or more [1(1)(i)]. Additionally, if the accused has been previously convicted of an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for seven years or more, or has been convicted on two or more occasions of a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for three years or more but less than seven years, bail is not granted [1(1)(ii)]. 

Furthermore, for non-bailable offences, the court may impose conditions such as attendance as per bond conditions, not committing a similar offence, and not tampering with evidence [1(3)]. 

Importantly, the mere fact that an accused may be required for identification or for police custody beyond 15 days is not sufficient to deny bail, provided the person is otherwise entitled to bail and gives an undertaking to comply with directions [1(1)(4)]. 

However, in cases where the offence is punishable with death, life imprisonment, or seven years or more, the public prosecutor must be given an opportunity of hearing before bail is granted [1(1)(5)].

Thus, the key difference is that bailable offences allow for bail without stringent conditions, while non-bailable offences restrict bail and require strict conditions, including prior convictions, severity of the offence, and judicial discretion.

The difference between bail in bailable and non-bailable offences lies in the legal framework governing their availability and conditions for release.

A "bailable offence" is defined as an offence that is shown as bailable in the First Schedule or made bailable by any other law in force. A "non-bailable offence" means any other offence not falling under a bailable offence [4(c)]. 

According to Section 478(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, when a person is not accused of a non-bailable offence, they may be released on bail if they are prepared to give bail, and if they are indigent, they may be discharged on a bond for appearance [6]. This provision applies to persons not accused of non-bailable offences, implying that bail is more readily available in bailable offences.

In contrast, Section 480(1)(i) and (ii) of the same Sanhita states that a person accused of or suspected of a non-bailable offence shall not be released on bail if there are reasonable grounds to believe they committed an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment, or if the offence is cognizable and they have a prior conviction for imprisonment of seven years or more or for two or more cognizable offences punishable with imprisonment of three years or more but less than seven years [1]. This shows that bail is strictly restricted in non-bailable offences.

Additionally, Section 480(3) mandates that when bail is granted under sub-section (1) for a non-bailable offence, the Court must impose conditions such as attendance as per bond conditions, not committing a similar offence, and not tampering with evidence [1]. These conditions are not required in bailable offences, as they are not subject to such restrictions.

Moreover, Section 478(1) allows bail for persons not accused of non-bailable offences, while Section 480 governs bail for those accused of non-bailable offences, indicating a fundamental difference in the availability and conditions of bail.

Thus, the key difference is that bailable offences allow bail without strict conditions and are generally available to all persons, whereas non-bailable offences restrict bail under strict conditions and only allow release when there are no reasonable grounds to believe guilt or when special circumstances apply, such as being a child, woman, or sick person [1].
